blocks.text: A 16 mm thick steel boiler drum holds steam at 8 MPa. If a fatigue crack grows through the wall, one of two things happens: the steam leaks out in a small jet that operators can hear and see, or the crack runs the length of the drum in an instant. Which one it is depends on a simple comparison between two lengths.

blocks.markdown: Many pressure vessels and pipes are designed so that a growing crack gets through the wall **while it is still short**. A through-wall crack that is shorter than its critical size releases fluid, which is detected by leakage monitoring, and the plant is shut down safely. This is the **leak-before-break (LBB)** idea. It works only if the critical length of a through-wall crack is clearly larger than the wall thickness, so that the crack penetrates the wall before it can run unstably.

blocks.title: Leak-before-break
blocks.text: A vessel satisfies leak-before-break when a part-through crack growing in the thickness direction becomes a through-wall (leaking) crack whose length is still below the critical length for fast fracture. As a screening rule, we require the critical through-wall half-length $a_c$ to exceed the wall thickness $t$ by a margin (here we use $a_c \ge 2t$ as an illustrative margin; actual rules vary by industry and standard).

blocks.caption: Hoop (circumferential) stress in a thin-walled cylinder: internal pressure $p$, mean radius $r$, wall thickness $t$. Axial stress is half of this, so hoop stress drives axial cracks.
Critical half-length of a through-wall crack (simplified, $Y = 1$, ignoring shell bulging; this is mildly unconservative, and real assessments apply a correction).

blocks.title: A vessel that satisfies LBB
blocks.prompt: A cylindrical vessel has mean radius 0.5 m, wall thickness 20 mm and internal pressure 6 MPa. Its steel has an assumed toughness $K_c = 100$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$. Check LBB using $a_c\ge 2t$.

steps.text: Compare with $2t = 40$ mm: 141 mm is well above 40 mm, so the crack will leak long before it becomes critical.

blocks.answer: $a_c\approx141$ mm, about 7.1 times the wall thickness: LBB is satisfied.

rows: Safe-life
Component is crack-free at start; fatigue life is predicted and a scatter factor applied
Retire at a fraction of calculated or tested life
Landing gear, engine discs, rotating parts
Fail-safe
Cracks may form; structure carries load after a member fails
Redundant load paths, crack arrest, inspection
Aircraft skins and wings
Damage tolerance / LBB
Cracks of a given size exist; growth is predicted
Inspection intervals; leak detection before break
Pressure vessels, piping
blocks.caption: Three design philosophies for flaw tolerance.

blocks.markdown: **Safe-life versus fail-safe.** Safe-life design makes no allowance for undetected cracks. It uses an experimental or calculated fatigue life divided by a scatter factor, then removes the part regardless of its condition. It is simple but wasteful and has no defence if an unexpected flaw is present. Fail-safe design accepts that a member may crack and ensures the remaining structure can carry the load until the next inspection. It needs redundancy and inspection access.

blocks.title: A vessel that fails the LBB criterion, and a re-rating
blocks.prompt: A vessel has mean radius 0.4 m and wall thickness 16 mm at 8 MPa. The steel has $K_c = 50$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$. (a) Check $a_c \ge 2t$. (b) What pressure would just meet it?

steps.text: So LBB is not met with margin. For $a_c = 0.032$ m the allowed hoop stress is $K_c/\sqrt{\pi a_c}$.

blocks.answer: At 8 MPa the criterion fails ($a_c\approx19.9$ mm); re-rating to about 6.31 MPa would meet it.

rows: Flaws far below the critical size and slow growth
Continue in service with monitoring
Adequate margin
Margin inadequate but reducible
Re-rate (lower pressure or temperature) or repair
Reducing stress raises $a_c$ as $\sigma^{-2}$
Flaws near critical, fast growth, or no practical repair
Retire (replace)
Risk of unstable fracture is not acceptable

items: Lower stress gives a much bigger critical crack: $a_c\propto\sigma_h^{-2}$.
A tougher steel increases $a_c$ as $K_c^2$ and favours LBB.
Re-rating trades output for safety margin; repair removes the flaw; retirement is chosen when neither can restore margin.

blocks.title: LBB needs leak detection and a ductile material
blocks.text: LBB is valid only if leakage is detected in time and the toughness is high enough at the operating temperature. For brittle or cold-embrittled steels, or where leakage cannot be monitored, a vessel should not be justified on LBB.

points: Hoop stress $\sigma_h=pr/t$ drives axial through-wall cracks; $a_c=(1/\pi)(K_c/\sigma_h)^2$.
LBB holds if the critical through-wall length comfortably exceeds the wall thickness so a leak appears first.
Safe-life retires parts by calculated life with a scatter factor; fail-safe tolerates a member failure through redundancy; when margin is lost choose repair, re-rate or retire.

questions.stem: What does a vessel designed on a leak-before-break basis rely on?

options.text: A crack grows through the wall and leaks while still shorter than the critical length for fast fracture
A crack never grows because the stress is below the threshold
The vessel is always replaced before any crack could form
The vessel is made so thick that stress is zero

questions.correctOptionText: A crack grows through the wall and leaks while still shorter than the critical length for fast fracture

distractorRationale.a: Correct: leakage gives warning before unstable fracture.
distractorRationale.d: Stress is never zero in a pressurised vessel.

questions.explanation: LBB means a through-wall crack reaches the surface and leaks at a size below its critical length, so operators detect the leak and shut down before any rapid fracture. It therefore assumes cracks may exist and grow.

options.text: The part is retired after a fraction of its calculated life without inspection
The part is made of a material with infinite toughness
The structure can carry the load after one member fails, through redundancy, until the failure is found
No cracks are assumed to exist ever

questions.correctOptionText: The structure can carry the load after one member fails, through redundancy, until the failure is found

distractorRationale.c: Correct: fail-safe allows failure of a member without loss of the structure.

questions.explanation: A fail-safe structure has alternative load paths so one cracked member does not cause the whole to fail. Inspection finds the damage before the remaining members are overloaded.

questions.stem: The operating pressure of a thin-walled cylinder is halved while all else is unchanged. What happens to the critical through-wall half-length for fracture?

options.text: It increases by a factor of 2
It decreases by a factor of 2
It increases by a factor of 4
It is unchanged

questions.correctOptionText: It increases by a factor of 4

distractorRationale.b: Lower stress increases the tolerable crack.
distractorRationale.d: The critical size depends on stress.

questions.explanation: The hoop stress is proportional to the pressure and $a_c\propto\sigma_h^{-2}$, so halving the pressure quadruples the critical crack size. This is why re-rating is an effective response when margin is short.

questions.stem: An assessment shows that a vessel with a stable, slowly growing flaw has insufficient margin at its present pressure, but adequate margin at 70 percent of that pressure. Replacement would take a year. Which decision is the most reasonable?

options.text: Continue unchanged because the flaw is stable
Immediately retire and scrap the vessel
Increase pressure to test the flaw
Re-rate to the lower pressure and monitor

questions.correctOptionText: Re-rate to the lower pressure and monitor

distractorRationale.a: Margin is inadequate at the current pressure.
distractorRationale.b: Retirement is not forced when a re-rate restores margin.
distractorRationale.c: Raising pressure would worsen the margin.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: re-rating restores the margin with little cost.

questions.explanation: A lower pressure reduces hoop stress and so increases the critical crack size, restoring margin while the vessel is monitored. Retirement would be chosen if no re-rating or repair restored an acceptable margin.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts safe-life with damage-tolerant methods?

options.text: Safe-life assumes a crack-free part and retires it with a scatter factor, while damage tolerance assumes flaws exist and manages them by inspection
Safe-life relies on inspection while damage tolerance does not
Safe-life and damage tolerance are the same
Damage tolerance assumes no flaws at all

questions.correctOptionText: Safe-life assumes a crack-free part and retires it with a scatter factor, while damage tolerance assumes flaws exist and manages them by inspection
questions.explanation: Safe-life depends on a calculated or test life and a scatter factor, with no inspection credit for cracks. Damage-tolerant design assumes a flaw of a given size exists and uses crack growth predictions with inspection to manage it.

questions.stem: A cylindrical air receiver has internal pressure 4 MPa, mean radius 0.3 m and wall thickness 12 mm. Find the hoop stress in MPa using $\sigma_h=pr/t$.
questions.explanation: $\sigma_h=4\times0.3/0.012=100$ MPa. Radius and thickness must be in the same unit, here metres.

questions.stem: A steel has $K_c = 90$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$ (assumed). It is loaded by a hoop stress of 180 MPa and contains a through-wall crack ($Y=1$). Find the critical half-length in mm.
questions.explanation: $a_c=(1/\pi)(90/180)^2=0.25/\pi=0.07958$ m, which is 79.6 mm. This is the half-length of the through-wall crack.

questions.stem: A vessel has mean radius 0.6 m, wall thickness 25 mm and steel toughness $K_c = 70$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$ (assumed). Using the illustrative criterion $a_c\ge 2t$, what is the maximum internal pressure in MPa for which leak-before-break is met? Take $Y=1$.
questions.explanation: The required $a_c=2t=0.050$ m, so $\sigma_h=K_c/\sqrt{\pi a_c}=70/\sqrt{\pi\times0.05}=176.6$ MPa. Then $p=\sigma_h t/r=176.6\times0.025/0.6=7.36$ MPa. Lower pressures give larger critical lengths and therefore satisfy the criterion.

questions.stem: Contrast safe-life and fail-safe design philosophies, giving one advantage and one limitation of each and one typical application.
markingGuide: Safe-life: crack-free start, life from test or calculation divided by a scatter factor, retire regardless of condition
Safe-life advantage: simple, no inspection needed; limitation: wasteful and no defence against unexpected flaws
Fail-safe: structure tolerates failure of a member via redundancy and crack arrest
Fail-safe advantage: tolerates damage between inspections; limitation: needs redundancy, weight and inspection access
Gives a sensible application for each (for example landing gear and aircraft skin)
questions.explanation: Safe-life puts all the trust in prediction and retires parts early, while fail-safe puts trust in redundancy and inspection. The two are chosen according to whether redundant load paths and inspection access can be provided.

questions.stem: A cylindrical vessel (mean radius 0.8 m, wall 30 mm) operates at 5 MPa; steel toughness is $K_c = 45$ MPa$\sqrt{\text{m}}$ (assumed). (a) Compute the hoop stress and critical through-wall half-length. (b) Decide whether leak-before-break with the margin $a_c\ge 2t$ is met. (c) Recommend repair, re-rate or retire and justify with a quantitative pressure.
markingGuide: Compares with $2t=60$ mm and concludes the margin is not met (only about 1.21 times $t$)
Recommends re-rating (or repair) rather than retirement if a modest pressure reduction restores margin
Finds the pressure giving $a_c=60$ mm as about 3.89 MPa and mentions leak detection
questions.explanation: The hoop stress is 133.3 MPa and the critical half-length is 36.3 mm, below the 60 mm required. Reducing pressure to about 3.89 MPa restores the margin, so re-rating (or repair) is justified rather than retirement.
